sentence_timing.text: The collapse of the Western Roman Empire was not a sudden event, but a century-long disintegration triggered by systemic failure.
Decades of civil war and economic crisis during the third century had already left the imperial infrastructure brittle.
Diocletian’s decision to divide the empire into East and West created a permanent administrative split, leaving the West increasingly vulnerable.
The westward expansion of the Huns pushed Germanic tribes toward Roman borders, culminating in the catastrophic Roman defeat at the Battle of Adrianople in 378.
By 410, the unthinkable occurred when Alaric and the Visigoths sacked the city of Rome for the first time in eight centuries.
Internal stability crumbled as the military relied on foreign mercenaries, while the loss of North African grain supplies crippled the economy.
Finally, in 476, the Germanic chieftain Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus.
By sending the imperial regalia to Constantinople, Odoacer effectively signaled the end of the Western Roman Empire.
